title: German panel discussion in partnership with the Weizenbaum Institute: register now!
content:
As part of #ossym 2026, we are delighted to invite you, in partnership with the Weizenbaum Institute, to an evening event featuring a panel discussion in Berlin. Please note that the event will be held entirely in German.

  • What: Panel discussion followed by networking (including snacks)
  • When: 8 October 2026, 7.00 pm
  • Where: Weizenbaum Institute, Hardenbergstrasse 23, 10623 Berlin

    • The development of competitive European services in the field of artificial intelligence – particularly in innovative approaches such as agent-based AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – requires access to valid, large-scale web data. At present, the value generated from this publicly accessible data on the internet is almost exclusively controlled by a handful of non-European monopolists. This lack of transparency poses massive risks for Europe: distorted information, one-sidedly trained AI models and products that do not reflect European values and legislation jeopardise our digital sovereignty and democratic discourse.

title: Google is once again in the pillory for favoring its own services
content:
In July 2026, the European Commission imposed a fine of 890 million euros on Google for, among other things, supposedly favoring its own search services, such as Google Shopping and Google Flights, over those of other providers, and thereby violating the Digital Markets Act (DMA).

The fine imposed is the highest the Commission has ever imposed for a violation of the DMA.

Read more about what the Commision‘s decision means, what happens next, and how the PriDi team assesses the fine that has now been imposed. Hop over to the PriDi project blog and get filled in on the details here. (Please Note: the blogpost is available in German language only.)

title: Various European Commission consultations
content:
An Open Web Data Infrastructure for Europe: We’re actively helping to shape European policy and legislation!

We completed the OpenWebSearch.EU project in April this year. Nevertheless, the OpenWebSearch Initiative, which brings together many partners from the OWS project and new stakeholders from research and industry, continues to work tirelessly on and for the Open Web Index (OWI).

The initiative not only aims to develop the infrastructure further, but is also committed to creating the framework conditions for a European Web Data Infrastructure. Shaping European policy and influencing legislation in support of an open European Web Data Infrastructure are, and will remain, key tasks of the initiative and the OSF.

We take every opportunity to emphasize the importance of a web data infrastructure for Europe!

With this mission in mind, we have, over the past few months, submitted comments on various European Commission consultations in collaboration with the OpenWebSearch Initiative and the PriDI project. In these consultations, citizens and other stakeholders can provide feedback on the Commission’s planned policy and legislative initiatives.

title: Law Enforcement against Big Tech – Still a Fight against Windmills?
content:
The PriDI team is currently reporting on two proceedings that require Google to make substantial payments. The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) upheld a fine imposed by the European Commission, and a court in Sweden ordered Google to pay damages.

The CJEU Ruling

The CJEU dealt with Google’s pre-installation agreements and licensing conditions. Under these, the manufacturers of Android smartphones and mobile network operators who wanted to integrate Google services on Android devices always had to install an entire package of Google apps. This included the Google browser Chrome and Google search.

The European Commission considered this obligation to be an abuse of Google’s dominant market position and imposed a fine on Google. The CJEU has now upheld the fine in the amount of €4.1 billion (Case No.: C-738/22 PP).

title: “Recognition of Open Source Work as Volunteer Work in Germany”
content:
Volunteer work is perceived as particularly fulfilling when its impact is immediately noticeable – for example, when working with people or animals. A smile, a step forward, a direct change: Such tangible results are motivating and make the value of the work clear to everyone involved.

But there are also forms of volunteer work whose impact is less visible and, for that very reason, is often underestimated. This includes contributing to open-source projects. The work often takes place behind closed doors, away from the spotlight; results are frequently abstract and therefore not always immediately apparent – but by no means less significant.

Boris Hinzer’s petition “Open Source as Volunteer Work” addresses precisely this issue: It aims to gain greater recognition for open-source work as volunteer engagement and to secure more social appreciation and support for it. As the Open Search Foundation, we support this important initiative with our vote.

What would actually happen if this work were to suddenly disappear?

title: Registration for #ossym2026 is now open
content:
The 8th International Open Search Symposium (#ossym) brings together experts and practitioners from across computer science, law and regulation, ethics, economics, and civil society.

#ossym2026 will take place as a hybrid event in Berlin from 7–9 October 2026, hosted at CODE University of Applied Sciences and supported by the German Aerospace Center (DLR). This year’s conference theme is “Boosting Digital Sovereignty.”
Join us for inspiring talks, thoughtful discussions, and the latest research on open and distributed web search, open web data infrastructure, and their role in AI.

We are especially interested in how an open web data infrastructure can counter the current concentration of web services, value loss, and regulatory pressure. Key questions include:

  • How can open web search and web data infrastructure strengthen digital diversity?
  • Which technical and economic concepts improve acceptance and resilience?
  • Which ethical and legal questions must be addressed to make this approach work?

    • Confirmed* keynote speakers include:

  • Stéphane Beemelmans (DLR)
  • Peter Gehle (DLR)
  • Julian Kunkel (GWDG / University of Göttingen)
  • Aline Blankertz (Structural Integrity)
  • Stefan Mesken (DeepL)

title: New SOURCE Project Launched
content:
Together with our project partners, the University of Passau, the University of Kassel, the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre (LRZ), and Alliance4Europe (A4E), we were successful in the competitive tendering process for this collaborative project within the BMFTR research program “Digital.Sicher.Souverän.”

The focus of SOURCE is the development of a freely accessible database of potential disinformation artifacts. This involves utilizing web data from the Open Web Index and additional social media crawls, which are then analyzed and interpreted in terms of content and origin using AI tools. The necessary AI, cloud, and storage capacities are provided by a federated digital infrastructure.

The active Open Web Search community, as well as technical and editorial expert communities, are brought on board early for needs assessments. The communities are expected to contribute concrete use cases, which will be used to test, further enrich, and make the database content practical.

title: Fighting the Search Monopoly with an Open Source Index: An Interview with Michael Granitzer from OpenWebSearch | Reset Digital for Good
content:
„Our mission is to break up the silo of a single search engine. (…) We’re doing this by crawling the web, collecting web pages, and preparing them to be consumed by search engines. Preparing them involves cleaning advertisements and navigation links, then extracting the main content. This index can be used by individuals or organisations to build their own search engines.“ states Michael.

While scaling up to compete with monopolies such as Google would require enormous resources, Michael believes that a community-oriented project could complement traditional and AI search as a public good. He envisions a future in which small AI models enable users to search for and combine information from various sources, independently of large technology companies.

„In an ideal scenario, the AI model is running on my machine and controlling my data. It’s a tool that helps me, conducts searches on my behalf and understands what I want to do. I’m talking about small language models rather than large language models. A model that helps me search, aggregate and synthesise information based on search endpoints that I choose.“, he states

title: Fact checking, smart search, and more: Nine partner projects show what the future of open web search could look like
content:
As a reminder, the OpenWebSearch.EU project was implemented by 14 partner organizations from the research and non-profit sectors and aimed to create the first European Open Web Index as the centerpiece for sovereign structured access to the internet.

The OWI (Open Web Index) has been up and running since June 2025 and has crawled an impressive 1.3 petabytes of data to this date. In the course of the project, a total of 15 third-party partner projects were integrated through various open calls. The goal: to conduct legal, technical, and commercial analysis and feasibility studies related to the Open Web Index in order to lay a solid foundation for the expansion of a European web data infrastructure.

Seven of the third-party partner projects (projects from Open Call 2) dealt with specific technical application examples based on the OWI. The projects demonstrate the range of possibilities when web index data is openly accessible. We have summarized the promising results briefly:
